cards.title: 2.1 The Structure of the Atom
body: An understanding of the structure of the atom and its interaction with energy helps in discoveries about matter.
Much of the study of modern physics is an attempt to understand the inner structure of the atom.
**An atom** is the smallest particle of an element which can take part in a chemical reaction.
**The nucleus** is the central core of an atom.
The nucleus is surrounded by electrons moving in orbits at various energy levels.

cards.title: 2.1 Atom — a picture good enough for this course
body: Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with electrons in energy levels around it. Electrons do not sit anywhere — they occupy allowed orbits / shells. Jumping between levels absorbs or emits a packet of light.

Study steps
body: 1. Read the key definition cards once without notes.
2. Cover the examples and say the rule in your own words.
3. Do the unit exercise; check each why-step before the next question.
4. Replay the match game until you can finish it without peeking.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following scientific figures is historically associated with the discovery of the electron in 1897?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Historical review of atomic structure**
John Dalton formulated early atomic theory. Ernest Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus. Niels Bohr introduced quantized orbits. J.J. Thomson discovered the electron using cathode ray tube experiments in 1897.

**Step 2: Conclusion**
Therefore, J.J. Thomson is the correct scientist.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In 1932, James Chadwick discovered which of the following subatomic particles?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Track subatomic discoveries**
The electron was discovered in 1897 by Thomson. The proton was identified by Rutherford in 1918. James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles.

**Step 2: Conclusion**
Thus, James Chadwick discovered the neutron.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which atomic model envisioned the atom as a uniform positive sphere with embedded negative electrons?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify model definitions**
The planetary model has orbiting electrons. The Bohr model introduces energy quantization. The Plum Pudding model, proposed by J.J. Thomson, describes electrons embedded in a uniform positive sphere.

**Step 2: Match**
Thus, the correct model is the Plum pudding model.

cards.title: 2.2 Particle–wave duality & the photon
body: Light behaves as a wave (interference, diffraction) *and* as particles called **photons**.
E = h f also E = h c / λ
h = Planck’s constant = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Higher frequency (bluer / UV) photons carry more energy. Radio photons are cheap and harmless one-by-one; X-ray photons are expensive.

cards.title: Mnemonic
body: Energy rides on frequency, not on “how bright”. Brightness = more photons, not fatter photons.

cards.title: 2.2.1 The Dual Nature of Light
body: A stone dropped into a lake (collision) and the ripples (wave motion) that spread out from its point of impact apparently have in common only the ability to carry energy and momentum from one place to another.
The concept that light travels as a series of little packets is directly opposed to the wave theory of light.
The wave theory of light explains diffraction and interference, which the quantum theory cannot account for.
The quantum theory explains the photoelectric effect, which the wave theory cannot account for.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Energy of a Photon
body: In the year 1865 James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879), Scottish physicist, proposed that light is a high frequency electromagnetic wave.
According to his theory the speed of these electromagnetic waves is 3×10⁸ m/s, which is in agreement with the measured value.
In his theory, he concluded that light is composed of corpuscles or discontinuous quanta of energy.
By increasing the intensity of the light of given wavelength, there is only an increase in the number of photons per second crossing a given area, with each photon having the same energy.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Photoelectric effect
body: When light hits some metals, electrons fly out — but only if the light’s frequency is above a **threshold frequency** f₀. Below that, even a very bright lamp does nothing. That wrecks the old wave-only model and is why Einstein used photons.
Kₘₐₓ = h f − φ
φ (work function) = minimum energy to free an electron = h f₀.

cards.title: One photon vs one electron. Extra energy becomes kinetic energy.
Raises Kₘₐₓ
body: Higher f (or shorter λ). Intensity does *not* change Kₘₐₓ.

cards.title: Raises number of electrons
body: Higher intensity (more photons per second) — but only if f ≥ f₀.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Photoelectric effect
body: Applications in the book: photocells, automatic doors / counters, solar exposure meters, sound-on-film, burglar alarms — anything that turns light into a current of electrons.

cards.title: Exercise E — photon energy
cards.problem: Violet light has frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find the energy of one photon. h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

steps.text: (Do not use ½mv² here — that is the electron later.) E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) × (7.5 × 10¹⁴). 6.63 × 7.5 = 49.725. 10⁻³⁴ × 10¹⁴ = 10⁻²⁰.
In electron-volts (optional extra): divide by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 3.1 eV.

cards.answer: In electron-volts (optional extra): divide by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 3.1 eV.

cards.title: Exercise F — photoelectric
cards.problem: A metal has work function 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz shines on it. Find (i) whether electrons are emitted (ii) Kₘₐₓ.

steps.text: Threshold check equivalent: f₀ = φ/h = 3.2e-19 / 6.63e-34 ≈ 4.83×10¹⁴ Hz.
If the question had used a frequency below 4.83×10¹⁴ Hz, Kₘₐₓ would be “no emission”, not a negative number.

cards.answer: If the question had used a frequency below 4.83×10¹⁴ Hz, Kₘₐₓ would be “no emission”, not a negative number.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Photoelectric Effect
body: The phenomenon of photoelectric emission was discovered in 1887 by Heinrich Hertz, during his electromagnetic wave experiments.

In his experimental investigation, on the production of electromagnetic waves by means of a spark discharge, he observed that high voltage sparks across the detector loop were enhanced when the emitter (metal) plate was illuminated by ultraviolet light.

Lenard observed that when ultraviolet radiations were allowed to fall on the emitter plate, C (cathode) of an evacuated glass tube enclosing two electrodes (metal plates), current flows in the circuit.
As soon as the ultraviolet radiations were stopped, the current flow was also stopped.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Applications of Photoelectric Effect
body: **Photocell** is a device used to convert light energy into electric energy.
**Photocell** is an application of the photoelectric effect.
When the light of a suitable wavelength falls on emitter C, photoelectrons emit instantaneously from the emitter.
Owing to the ionization of the inert gas, the current strength is more and it is five to ten times stronger than the current from the vacuum type.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The strong nuclear force within an atomic nucleus acts between which of the following?

options.D: Between any two nucleons (protons or neutrons) at close range

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze strong nuclear force properties**
The strong nuclear force is charge-independent. It does not affect electrons, which are leptons.

**Step 2: Assess options**
It acts equally between proton-proton, neutron-neutron, and proton-neutron pairs at extremely short distances ($$< 10^{-15}\, \text{m}$$). Therefore, it acts between any two nucleons.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: According to the principle of wave-particle duality, light behaves as:

options.A: Exclusively a wave under all conditions
options.B: Exclusively a particle under all conditions
options.C: Both a wave and a particle depending on the experimental measurement
options.D: Neither a wave nor a particle

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand wave-particle duality**
Light displays wave properties (like interference) during propagation and particle properties (like photoelectric effect) during energy exchange with matter.

**Step 2: Identify matching statement**
Thus, it behaves as both wave and particle depending on the experiment.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: According to the principle of wave-particle duality, light behaves as:

steps.text: Light displays wave properties (like interference) during propagation and particle properties (like photoelectric effect) during energy exchange with matter.
Thus, it behaves as both wave and particle depending on the experiment.

cards.answer: C. Both a wave and a particle depending on the experimental measurement

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle is given by ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** De Broglie proposed that moving particles have wave properties.

**Step 2:** The wavelength equals Planck's constant divided by momentum.

**Step 3:** $\lambda = h/p = h/(mv)$.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: 2.3 Atomic Spectra
body: Newton found that the spectrum of sunlight is impure because the different-coloured images overlap.
A pure spectrum is one in which the different-coloured images contain only the light of one colour.
The spectrometer (spectroscope) can be used to provide a pure spectrum.
A spectroscope may consist of a narrow slit, a prism, and several lenses that straighten the light rays and magnify the spectrum.
A spectroscope measures wavelengths accurately using either a diffraction grating or a prism to separate different wavelengths of light.

cards.title: 2.3 Atomic spectra
body: A hot gas or a discharge tube gives **line emission spectra** — only certain colours. A cool gas in front of white light gives dark **absorption lines** at those same frequencies. Each element has a fingerprint because its allowed electron jumps are unique.

cards.title: Jump story
body: Electron falls down a level → emits a photon of exactly that energy gap. Electron climbs up → absorbs that photon. No in-between colours.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What fundamental physical constant relates the energy of a photon to the frequency of its electromagnetic wave?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the energy formula**
$$E = hf$$

**Step 2: Identify constant $$h$$**
$$h$$ is defined as Planck's constant ($$6.63 \times 10^{-34}\, \text{J}\cdot\text{s}$$). This constant relates a photon's energy to its wave frequency.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the photoelectric effect, if the frequency of the incident light is below the threshold frequency:

options.A: Electrons are emitted with very low kinetic energy
options.B: No electrons are emitted, regardless of the light intensity
options.C: Electrons are emitted after a long time lag

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze quantum threshold rules**
If $$f < f_0$$, the energy of each incident photon ($$hf$$) is strictly less than the metal's work function ($$\phi_0$$).

**Step 2: Deduce outcomes**
Because the interaction is strictly one-on-one (one photon to one electron), no individual electron can gather enough energy to escape, regardless of how many photons hit the surface per second (intensity). Thus, **no electrons are emitted**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: In the photoelectric effect, if the frequency of the incident light is below the threshold frequency:

steps.text: If $$f < f_0$$, the energy of each incident photon ($$hf$$) is strictly less than the metal's work function ($$\phi_0$$).

Because the interaction is strictly one-on-one (one photon to one electron), no individual electron can gather enough energy to escape, regardless of how many photons hit the surface per second (intensity). Thus, **no electrons are emitted**.

cards.answer: B. No electrons are emitted, regardless of the light intensity

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom drops from a higher energy level to a lower one. What happens?

options.B: A photon is emitted with energy equal to the difference between the levels

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Energy levels in atoms are fixed (quantised).

**Step 2:** When the electron falls, the atom loses energy $\Delta E$.

**Step 3:** This energy is emitted as a photon with $hf = \Delta E$, giving a line in the emission spectrum.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

Spectroscopy is the technique of analysing light and correlating the analysis with the nature of the light source.

tips.text: An atom is composed of electrons, protons, and neutrons.
The protons and neutrons are the constituent particles of the nucleus, which is the central core of an atom.
The notations, respectively, Z, A, and N are used to represent the atomic number, mass number and neutron number, respectively.
The force that keeps the neutrons and protons within the nucleus is called the nuclear force. This force is greater than the force of repulsion between protons–protons at short range.
Atoms differ in kind by their atomic number.
Electromagnetic radiation and electrons have a dual nature. They behave as particles and as wave motion.
Einstein proposed in his theory that light is composed of corpuscles or discontinuous quanta of energy called “photons”.
Photons are electrically neutral and are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
The phenomenon of the emission of electrons from a metal surface when a radiation of suitable frequency incidents on it is known as the “photoelectric effect”.
The minimum frequency of the radiation required for electron emission is called the threshold frequency.
Raises Kₘₐₓ: Higher f (or shorter λ). Intensity does not change Kₘₐₓ.
Raises number of electrons: Higher intensity (more photons per second) — but only if f ≥ f₀.

questions.answer: Electrons are emitted instantly only if each photon's energy hf exceeds the work function; below the threshold frequency no electrons come out however intense the light, which a wave model cannot explain.
why: In the wave model, any frequency should eventually eject electrons if the light is bright enough.
Experiments show a threshold frequency and instant emission.
This fits light arriving in packets (photons) of energy $hf$, each absorbed by one electron.
